entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Enentarzi was ensi (governor-priest) of Lagash in mid-third-millennium BCE Sumer, remembered as a chief priest of the god Ningirsu who also exercised civic authority. His tenure belongs to the era when temple estates, irrigation labour, and scribal administration defined city-state power in southern Mesopotamia.

Lagash’s politics intertwined cult and palace: control of Ningirsu’s temple meant control of land, rations, and prestige in contests with rival cities such as Umma. Enentarzi’s priestly title signals how religious office could be the spine of economic government before later royal ideologies fully separated king from temple.

Cuneiform archives make figures like Enentarzi crucial for reconstructing early bureaucracy—rations lists, land grants, and cultic offerings that reveal Sumerian statecraft from the ground up.
